prompt:
Research what the Rust project officially documents about its release cadence and how long each stable version is supported. Cite the official Rust page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
The Rust project follows a predictable, time-based release model with a very specific support window for each stable version. The language ships a new stable release every six weeks, but each individual stable version is only actively supported until the subsequent stable release is made. 

This means that while new versions come out every 42 days, each specific version has a support lifespan of exactly 6 weeks. After the next version is released, the previous version no longer receives bug fixes or security patches. It is worth noting that this 6-week support window applies to the compiler and standard library; the Rust project also provides longer, separate support windows for certain editions (which have their own lifecycles) and specific critical libraries (like the `regex` crate), but the stable compiler version itself is only supported until the next one arrives.

Here are the official documented claims:

SOURCE: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/appendix-07-nightly-rust.html | QUOTE: "Rust releases a new stable version every six weeks." | CLAIM: The official release cadence of the Rust project is every six weeks.
SOURCE: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/appendix-07-nightly-rust.html | QUOTE: "each stable release is only supported until the next stable release comes out" | CLAIM: Each stable version of Rust is supported for exactly 6 weeks (i.e., until the subsequent release replaces it).
